lessons.title: History and Evolution of Robotics
lessons.body: Robotics didn't start with shiny humanoids. In Africa, the roots go back to ancient automata and traditional craft. For example, the Egyptian water clock by Ctesibius around 270 BC used mechanical figures. But modern robotics began in the 1950s with Unimate, the first industrial robot, installed at General Motors in 1961. It weighed 2 tons and cost $25,000. In Africa, the first robots arrived in the 1980s in South African gold mines for drilling and in Egyptian textile factories for packaging. Today, countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and Rwanda are building local robotics startups. For instance, in 2020, a team in Nairobi built a robot to sort recyclable plastics using Arduino and servo motors. To understand this evolution, start by tracing key milestones: 1961 Unimate, 1970s Stanford Arm, 1990s mobile robots like Sojourner on Mars, and 2010s collaborative robots (cobots). In your workshop, create a timeline on a wall using cardboard and markers. Mark five events: first industrial robot, first mobile robot, first humanoid (ASIMO in 2000), first African robotics competition (2015 in South Africa), and first locally made robot in your country. Then, disassemble a simple toy robot or a broken DVD player to see how gears and motors work. This hands-on look shows that robotics is not magicâit's engineering that evolves step by step. Document your findings in a notebook: note the year, the inventor, and the country. This history lesson gives you context for why robots look and work the way they do today.

lessons.title: Types of Robots: Industrial, Mobile, Humanoid
lessons.body: Robots come in three main types, each suited to different jobs. Industrial robots are fixed in place and do repetitive tasks with high precision. In South Africa's automotive plants, KUKA robots weld car frames 24/7, lifting 200 kg payloads with 0.1 mm accuracy. They cost between $20,000 and $100,000. Mobile robots move aroundâlike drones, autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs), and rovers. In Kenya, Zipline drones deliver blood to rural clinics, covering 80 km in 30 minutes. AGVs in Moroccan warehouses move pallets using line-following sensors. Humanoid robots look like humans and are the hardest to build. They walk on two legs, use arms with multiple joints, and interact with people. Examples include Hanson Robotics' Sophia and Honda's ASIMO. In Africa, humanoid research is still emerging; a lab at the University of Cape Town built a small walking robot in 2019 using 12 servo motors and an Arduino Mega. To explore these types, build a simple mobile robot first: use a plastic chassis, two DC motors with wheels, an L298N motor driver, and an ultrasonic sensor. Program it to avoid obstacles. Then, convert it into a stationary industrial arm by replacing wheels with a gripper and a base. For humanoid, start with a bipedal walker kit. Compare their degrees of freedom (DOF): industrial 6 DOF, mobile 2-3 DOF, humanoid 20+ DOF. Choose the type based on your task: welding? industrial. Delivery? mobile. Customer service? humanoid. In your community, identify one task that a robot could doâlike sorting maize or fetching waterâand decide which type fits best. Write a one-page proposal with cost estimates.

lessons.title: Key Components of a Robot: Sensors, Actuators, Controllers
lessons.body: Every robot has three core parts: sensors, actuators, and a controller. Sensors are the robot's eyes and ears. Common types include ultrasonic (HC-SR04, $2) for distance, infrared (Sharp GP2Y0A21, $10) for proximity, and temperature (LM35, $1) for heat. In African farms, soil moisture sensors (capacitive, $5) help robots decide when to water. Actuators are the musclesâthey create motion. DC motors ($3) spin wheels, servo motors (SG90, $3) rotate arms to precise angles, and stepper motors (NEMA 17, $15) move 3D printer beds. In Ghana, a startup uses 12V DC motors to drive a solar-powered weeding robot. The controller is the brain. Popular choices: Arduino Uno ($25), Raspberry Pi 4 ($35), and ESP32 ($10). Arduino is best for beginners because it's cheap and has many tutorials. To see these parts in action, build a line-following robot. You need: 2 IR sensors, 2 DC motors with wheels, an L298N driver, an Arduino Uno, and a 9V battery. Wire the sensors to analog pins A0 and A1, motors to digital pins 5,6,9,10. Write code: if left sensor sees black, turn left; if right sees black, turn right; else go straight. Test on a black tape line. If the robot veers off, adjust sensor sensitivity with a potentiometer. For a challenge, add an ultrasonic sensor to stop when an obstacle is 10 cm away. Document each component's voltage and current: motors draw 200 mA each, sensors 15 mA, Arduino 50 mA. Total current must not exceed your battery's capacity. This hands-on project teaches you to identify and connect real parts.

lessons.title: Robot Applications in Industry and Society
lessons.body: Robots are already working across Africa. In South African mines, automated drills and loaders operate in dangerous tunnels, reducing human exposure to rockfalls. In Nigerian oil refineries, robots inspect pipelines for leaks, saving $1 million per incident. In Kenyan agriculture, a robot called "Shamba" uses a camera and machine learning to identify and pick ripe tomatoes, increasing yield by 20%. In healthcare, Rwandan hospitals use Zipline drones to deliver 150,000 blood units per year, cutting delivery time from 4 hours to 30 minutes. In education, Ghanaian schools use LEGO Mindstorms kits to teach coding. In society, robots assist people with disabilities: a Moroccan startup built a wheelchair with ultrasonic sensors that avoids obstacles and climbs curbs. In waste management, a South African robot sorts plastic, glass, and metal at 2 tons per hour. To apply robotics in your community, follow these steps: 1) Identify a problemâe.g., water fetching, crop monitoring, or security. 2) Research existing solutions and costs. 3) Build a prototype with cheap parts. For example, a solar-powered water pump robot can be made with a 12V pump, a soil moisture sensor, and an Arduino. 4) Test it for one week. 5) Calculate return on investment: if the robot costs $200 and saves 10 hours of labor per week at $2/hour, payback is 10 weeks. Document your results. Many African governments now offer grants for agri-robotics. In Kenya, the Kenya Industrial Research and Development Institute (KIRDI) funds prototypes up to $5,000. Write a proposal with a clear problem, solution, budget, and timeline. This lesson shows that robotics is not just for factoriesâit solves real African challenges.

lessons.title: Safety Standards and Ethical Considerations
lessons.body: Robots can hurt people if not designed safely. In 2015, a worker at a Volkswagen plant in Germany died when a robot crushed him against a metal plate. That's why safety standards exist. ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 cover industrial robot safety. They require emergency stop buttons, safety fences, and light curtains. In Africa, South Africa adopted SANS 10218, and Nigeria uses NIS 10218. For mobile robots, ISO 13482 covers personal care robots. Ethical issues include job displacement, privacy, and bias. In South Africa, mining robots replaced 5,000 jobs between 2010 and 2020, but created 1,200 new technical roles. In Kenya, drones used for delivery must respect privacyâno flying over private homes without consent. To build safe robots, follow these rules: 1) Always include a physical emergency stop that cuts power to motors. 2) Use low voltage (12V or less) for beginner projects. 3) Add bump sensors or ultrasonic sensors to detect humans. 4) Test in an open area away from people. 5) Label all wires and moving parts. For ethical design, ask: Who benefits? Who could be harmed? For example, a robot that sorts job applications might inherit human bias if trained on biased data. In your workshop, practice a safety drill: build a simple robot with a motor, then simulate a failure by disconnecting a sensor. Observe what happens. Then, add a kill switch. Write a one-page safety checklist for your robot, including: battery type, max speed, emergency stop location, and operating zone. Share it with your team. Remember, a safe robot is a useful robot.

lessons.title: Lab: Disassembling and Identifying Robot Parts
lessons.body: In this lab, you will take apart a broken robot or electronic toy and identify its components. You need: a broken RC car, toy robot, or old printer; a small Phillips screwdriver; a multimeter; a notebook; and safety goggles. Work on a clean, well-lit table. Start by removing batteries. Then, unscrew the casing. Take photos at each step. Inside, you'll find: 1) DC motorsâsmall cylindrical motors with two wires. Test with a multimeter: set to continuity, touch probes to wires; if it beeps, the motor is good. 2) Gearsâplastic or metal wheels that transfer motion. Count the teeth: a 10-tooth gear driving a 50-tooth gear gives 5:1 reduction, increasing torque. 3) Circuit boardâlook for the microcontroller (a black chip), resistors (color bands), capacitors (cylinders), and connectors. 4) Sensorsâin an RC car, you might find an infrared receiver or a bump switch. 5) Battery holderânote the voltage (usually 3V to 9V). 6) Wiresâtrace them from motors to the board. Draw a schematic in your notebook. For example, a typical RC car has: battery (+) â switch â board â motor driver â two motors. After disassembly, clean each part with a dry brush. Test motors with a 1.5V AA battery: touch wires to battery terminals; the motor should spin. If not, it's dead. Sort parts into labeled containers: motors, gears, sensors, boards, screws. Now, reassemble the robot in a new way: add a second motor to make a simple car. Or use the board to control an LED. Document what you learned: list three parts and their functions. This lab builds your confidence to repair and innovate. Remember, many great robots start from salvaged parts. Take clear notesâyou'll need them for Module 2.

quiz.q: What was the first industrial robot, installed in 1961?
quiz.explanation: Unimate was the first industrial robot, installed at General Motors in 1961.

quiz.q: Which African country adopted SANS 10218 for robot safety?
quiz.explanation: South Africa adopted SANS 10218, based on ISO 10218, for industrial robot safety.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of an Arduino Uno controller?
quiz.explanation: Arduino Uno is a popular beginner controller costing around $25.

quiz.q: Which sensor is used to measure distance in a robot?
quiz.explanation: HC-SR04 is an ultrasonic sensor used for distance measurement.

quiz.q: What does a servo motor do?
options: B) Rotate to a precise angle
quiz.explanation: Servo motors rotate to a specific angle based on a control signal.

quiz.q: In which year did Zipline start delivering blood in Rwanda?
quiz.explanation: Zipline began blood delivery in Rwanda in 2016.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mobile robot?
quiz.explanation: Zipline drone is a mobile robot that moves through the air.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an emergency stop button on a robot?
options: B) To cut power to motors
quiz.explanation: Emergency stop immediately cuts power to prevent accidents.

quiz.q: Which component is the 'brain' of a robot?
quiz.explanation: The controller, like Arduino or Raspberry Pi, processes sensor data and commands actuators.

quiz.q: What does a 5:1 gear reduction do?
quiz.explanation: A 5:1 reduction increases torque by 5 times while reducing speed.

quiz.q: Which African country has a robotics competition that started in 2015?
quiz.explanation: South Africa hosted the first African robotics competition in 2015.

quiz.q: What is the typical voltage of a small DC motor in a toy robot?
quiz.explanation: Small DC motors in toys usually operate between 3V and 6V.

quiz.q: Which safety standard covers personal care robots?
quiz.explanation: ISO 13482 specifically covers personal care robots.

quiz.q: What is a common use of robots in South African mines?
quiz.explanation: Automated drills and loaders are used in South African mines.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to test a motor's continuity?
quiz.explanation: A multimeter set to continuity can test if a motor's coil is intact.

quiz.q: What is the first step when disassembling a robot?
quiz.explanation: Always remove batteries first to prevent electric shock or short circuits.

quiz.q: Which of these is an ethical concern with robots?
quiz.explanation: Job displacement is a major ethical concern as robots automate tasks.

quiz.q: What does an L298N module do?
quiz.explanation: L298N is a motor driver that allows a microcontroller to control DC motors.

quiz.q: In Kenya, what does the Zipline drone deliver?
quiz.explanation: Zipline drones deliver blood to rural clinics in Kenya and Rwanda.

quiz.q: What is the typical payload of an industrial robot like KUKA?
quiz.explanation: Industrial robots like KUKA can lift payloads up to 200 kg or more.

quiz.q: Which component converts electrical energy to mechanical motion?
quiz.explanation: Actuators, such as motors, convert electrical energy into motion.

quiz.q: What is a common material for robot chassis in beginner projects?
quiz.explanation: Plastic chassis are cheap, lightweight, and easy to modify for beginners.

quiz.q: Which sensor would you use to detect a black line?
quiz.explanation: Infrared sensors reflect differently off black and white surfaces, ideal for line following.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a gear in a robot?
options: B) To transfer motion and adjust torque
quiz.explanation: Gears transfer motion and can increase torque or speed.

quiz.q: Which African country uses robots for pipeline inspection?
quiz.explanation: Nigerian oil refineries use robots to inspect pipelines for leaks.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a line-following robot?
quiz.explanation: Assembling the chassis with motors and wheels is the first physical step.

quiz.q: Which of these is a humanoid robot?
quiz.explanation: ASIMO is a humanoid robot developed by Honda.

quiz.q: What is the typical current draw of a small DC motor?
quiz.explanation: Small DC motors typically draw around 200 mA at 6V.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label wires when disassembling a robot?
options: A) To make it look neat
B) To remember connections for reassembly
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps you reconnect wires correctly when reassembling.

quiz.q: What is a potential benefit of using robots in African agriculture?
quiz.explanation: Robots like Shamba in Kenya can increase crop yield by 20% through precise picking.
